insider_note: Fullerene is a cage, so the note is a description of a cage: how many rings of each size, how they are fused, where the carbon atoms sit, and what each carbon does with its four valence electrons.

steps.label: What fullerenes are
lines: Fullerenes are a crystalline allotrope
of carbon, counted alongside diamond
and graphite.
The best known fullerene is C₆₀, a cage
of sixty carbon atoms.
C₆₀ is called buckminsterfullerene, and
also a bucky ball.
Unlike diamond and graphite it is made
of separate molecules.
steps.why: Diamond and graphite are giant structures with no molecules in them, so naming fullerene as a molecule is the first real difference. Everything else in the note describes the shape of that molecule.
common_mistakes: Leaving fullerene out of the crystalline forms. Diamond and graphite are the two always named, and NCERT counts the fullerenes as crystalline too.
Writing the formula as C₇₀ or C₆₀₀. The fullerene described here is C₆₀.
steps.memory_tip: C₆₀, buckminsterfullerene or bucky ball, the third crystalline allotrope of carbon.
steps.margin_note: Open with the formula and both names before describing the cage.

steps.label: Preparation
lines: Fullerenes are made by heating graphite
strongly in an electric arc in an
atmosphere of helium or argon.
The graphite is vaporised, and the
carbon vapour condenses to the cage
molecules.
Helium and argon are inert gases, and
they are used so that the hot carbon
does not burn.
steps.why: The preparation explains why fullerene was found so late: the cage forms only from free carbon vapour, and carbon vapour can be kept only in an atmosphere that will not react with it.
common_mistakes: Writing that fullerene is made by heating graphite in air. Carbon would burn; an inert gas such as helium or argon is used.
Writing that fullerene is made from diamond. The starting material is graphite.
steps.memory_tip: Graphite in an electric arc under helium or argon gives the fullerene cage.
steps.margin_note: Name the inert gas, since that is the part of the preparation easiest to forget.

steps.label: The rings of the cage
lines: The cage of C₆₀ is built from rings of
carbon atoms.
There are twenty six-membered rings and
twelve five-membered rings, thirty-two
rings in all.
A six-membered ring is fused either to
another six-membered ring or to a
five-membered ring.
A five-membered ring is fused only to
six-membered rings; two five-membered
rings are never fused to each other.
The twelve five-membered rings are what
curve the sheet of six-membered rings
round into a closed cage.
steps.why: A sheet of six-membered rings alone stays flat, as it does in graphite. The twelve five-membered rings are what bend it, and the rule that no two of them are fused is what spreads that bending evenly over the whole cage.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two counts. There are twenty six-membered rings and twelve five-membered rings.
Writing that two five-membered rings are fused to each other. A five-membered ring is fused only to six-membered rings.
Writing sixty as a ring count. Sixty is the number of carbon atoms, not of rings.
steps.memory_tip: Twenty six-membered and twelve five-membered rings, and no two five-membered rings together.
steps.margin_note: Write the two counts first and the fusion rule after them, as two separate statements.

steps.label: The sixty carbon atoms
lines: The cage has sixty vertices, and one
carbon atom sits at each of them.
That is why the molecule is C₆₀.
Three rings meet at every vertex, so
every carbon atom of the cage has the
same surroundings as every other.
steps.why: Sixty is a count of vertices rather than of rings, and that is the number most often misplaced. Because three rings meet at each vertex, all sixty carbon atoms are alike, which is why one description of the bonding covers the whole molecule.
common_mistakes: Writing that the sixty carbon atoms are of different kinds. Every vertex of the cage is the same, so all sixty carbon atoms are alike.
Confusing the sixty vertices with the thirty-two rings. They are two different counts.
steps.memory_tip: Sixty vertices, one carbon atom at each, and three rings meeting at every one.
steps.margin_note: Separate the count of vertices from the count of rings; they are easily mixed up.

steps.label: Bonding and hybridisation
lines: Each carbon atom is sp² hybridised.
It forms three sigma bonds to three
neighbouring carbon atoms.
The fourth valence electron of each
carbon atom lies in an unhybridised p
orbital and is delocalised over the
whole cage.
That delocalisation gives fullerene
aromatic character.
steps.why: The carbon atoms of fullerene do the same thing as those of graphite: three sigma bonds and one delocalised electron. The difference is only that the sheet is closed into a cage, so the delocalised electrons spread over a surface that has no edge.
common_mistakes: Writing sp³. That is the state of carbon in diamond, where each carbon atom is bonded to four others.
Writing that all four valence electrons are in sigma bonds. Three are; the fourth is delocalised.
steps.memory_tip: Three sigma bonds and one delocalised electron per carbon atom, the same count as in graphite.
steps.margin_note: State the hybridisation and then say where the fourth electron goes.

steps.label: The two bond lengths
lines: The C–C bonds of C₆₀ are not all of one
length.
There are two C–C distances:
So the cage is not a regular solid with
identical edges, even though all sixty
carbon atoms are alike.
steps.why: The two distances are a real measured difference and they are worth stating because they qualify the picture of a perfectly regular cage. The carbon atoms are all equivalent, but the bonds between them are of two kinds.
common_mistakes: Writing one bond length for the whole cage. There are two C–C distances, 143.5 pm and 138.3 pm.
Writing 141.5 pm or 154 pm here. Those are the C–C distances in graphite and in diamond.
steps.memory_tip: Two C–C distances in C₆₀: 143.5 pm and 138.3 pm.
steps.margin_note: Write both figures with the unit; one figure alone leaves the point of the step unmade.

steps.label: Conclusion
lines: So sixty sp² carbon atoms, twelve
five-membered rings and twenty
six-membered rings make one closed
cage, and the delocalised fourth
electrons give it aromatic character.

lines.text: Fullerene C₆₀ is a cage of sp² carbons

steps.why: The closing lines gather the counts and the bonding into one sentence, so that the note ends as a description of a single molecule rather than as a list of separate figures.
common_mistakes: Closing with the ring counts alone. The bonding and the aromatic character are part of what was asked for.
Closing by calling fullerene a giant structure. It is a molecule of sixty carbon atoms.
steps.memory_tip: Sixty sp² carbon atoms in thirty-two rings, with the fourth electrons delocalised.
steps.margin_note: Close by naming the cage and the aromatic character together.
